rv.q: Eurotrash *is* a good time, and if you find a better time in a theatre this season then it's going to be one hell of a Christmas.
This uproariously funny Young Vic show has absolutely nothing in common with the squalid late-night Channel 4 show of the same name.

It’s all the freewheeling and dysfunction that comes before that shows up the truth of difficult families, where love and hate and a desperate desire to stop your mother downing vodka before 11am can entertainingly co-exist.
Now it hits the English stage: Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter (whose scenes in Black Doves are a highlight of the Netflix spy series) attain Alpine heights of theatrical delight at the Young Vic.
Hunter is magnificent: fierce, frail, formidable.
What you get instead is the strange accomplishment of brilliant streaks of drama in a story with holes.
While her music leaks from its protective panels, what Eurotrash wants to say in its mockery of obscene wealth remains obscure, and so for all the flashiness, it makes no statement at all.
The result, in truth, is lukewarm.
The bag of make-believe faeces that splashes onto the stage towards the end of the evening turns out to be an all too apt metaphor for what we have had to endure.
Eurotrash grows into a moving meditation on family, resentment, trauma, and healing.
The energy of the duo is mind-blowing.
Witty and poignant, Eurotrash gets the standing ovation it deserves on press night.
It’s whirring, wise and wonderful, a gift not just for Christmas but for life.
Under director Walter Meierjohann’s guidance, the cast and creative team have generated an absurdist dynamic, which constantly surprises, tickles and unsettles.
Luckily, Whishaw and Turner have the star factor in spades — and together, they show us a great time.
Hunter is impossible to tear your eyes from: cruelly impish, eccentric and brisk, she has a bottomless vault of damaging insults to spew at her son in a rasping, husky voice.

Its ability to surprise and delight through miraculous writing and ingenious direction and the sensational performances from actors at the top of their game barely scratch the surface as to what makes this production so utterly exceptional.
It is an impressive piece of work.
As Mother, Kathryn Hunter is simply splendid, combining extraordinary physical comedy with a sharply judged sense of character.
This hilarious Euro-style show is a dream come true.
This hilarious Euro-style show is something of a dream come true.
Kracht’s book has been turned into a surreal and startlingly original piece of theatre by writer Colin Teevan and Dutch director Walter Meierjohann.
As a masterclass in stage acting and inspired production design, Eurotrash is a joy to watch.
Meierjohann’s entertaining 1hr 45min dramedy is performing at the Young Vic until 9 January 2027.
Walter Meierjohann’s production imaginatively draws out Kracht’s core theme of filthy lucre and the pair’s attempts to wipe clean their family’s shady past.
Hunter and Whishaw have great chemistry as an odd couple constantly bickering and eventually reconciling.
The journey on which the two characters embark is hilarious and ridiculously good fun...
Luckily, Whishaw and Hunter elevate the proceedings, matching the off-beat energy Meierjohann instils in the show.

Eurotrash is a brilliantly original show with a flawless cast that manages to deal with weighty issues of unethically obtained wealth, Europe's Nazi past, difficult parent-child relationships, sexual assault and trauma with a surprisingly light touch.
Eurotrash is also hugely funny as mother and son bicker 1 last time with life-altering revelations buried deep in their subconsciousnesses finally bubbling to the surface.
'Eurotrash' is a devilishly funny meditation on greed, guilt and reckoning.

Does the quirkiness sustain throughout the running time? I'm not sure it does quite fully. It did start to wear a little thin towards the end of the play, but there is so much else to enjoy about this production.
Instead, a mother and son who have spent a lifetime not talking finally find themselves sharing a summit, and the view, as the Swiss would surely be the first to point out, is worth every franc.
Whishaw and Hunter’s exquisite performances make them remarkably endearing and, to some degree, iconic.
On those terms it's satisfying because the stars absolutely deliver like you'd hope they would
A thoroughly entertaining production, ultimately lacking in enough substance to maintain the runtime.

cn.t: Whishaw and Hunter dazzle as a dysfunctional mother-son duo in this darkly funny Swiss road trip. Mostly rapturous reviews praise the leads' chemistry and sharp wit, though a few find the adaptation too surface-level.
